name: Theory of Mind
statement: To understand others, we grasp that they have beliefs and desires of their own, which may differ from ours.
meaning: Theory of mind is the capacity to attribute mental states, such as beliefs, desires, intentions, knowledge, and emotions, to oneself and to others, and to understand that other people have minds whose contents may differ from one's own. It is what allows us to predict and explain the behavior of others by reasoning about what they think, want, and feel, rather than only about what they physically do. The term was coined by David Premack and Guy Woodruff in a 1978 paper asking whether a chimpanzee has a theory of mind. In children, theory of mind is classically assessed with false-belief tasks, such as the Sally-Anne test, in which a child watches one character hide an object and leave while another moves it, and is then asked where the first character will look for it; passing requires understanding that the character holds a false belief about the object's location, and typically developing children begin to pass such tasks around the age of four. Theory of mind is a central concept in developmental psychology, cognitive science, autism research, and the study of animal cognition, underlying social understanding, communication, empathy, and deception.
mechanism: Theory of mind works by letting a person represent the mental states of others as distinct from reality and from their own mind, and use those representations to interpret behavior. To attribute a belief is to model that another person holds some picture of the world that guides their actions, even when that picture is mistaken. This is why the false-belief task is the classic test: understanding that someone will act on a belief that is false, and differs from what the observer knows to be true, requires genuinely representing the other's mind rather than simply reporting reality. In the Sally-Anne version, developed from the work of Wimmer and Perner and adapted by Baron-Cohen, Leslie, and Frith, a child sees Sally hide a marble and leave, sees Anne move it, and is asked where Sally will look; to answer correctly the child must set aside their own knowledge of the marble's true location and reason from Sally's outdated belief. Typically developing children come to pass such tasks around age four, which is taken to mark the emergence of an explicit theory of mind, though simpler, implicit sensitivity to others' beliefs appears earlier. The capacity supports a wide range of social abilities, including cooperation, communication, teaching, empathy, and deception, all of which depend on tracking what others know and want.

examples.text: A child who understands that Sally will look for her marble where she left it, not where it was secretly moved, has grasped a false belief.
Typically developing children begin to pass false-belief tasks around the age of four, marking an explicit theory of mind.
Premack and Woodruff coined the term in 1978 asking whether a chimpanzee attributes mental states to others.

variants.name: The false-belief task
variants.text: The classic test of theory of mind, requiring the child to predict action from a belief that is false and differs from reality.

variants.name: The autism hypothesis
variants.text: The influential but debated idea that autism involves difficulty with theory of mind, sometimes called mindblindness.

whyItMatters: Theory of mind is a central concept across the sciences of the mind, because the ability to attribute mental states to others underlies much of what makes human social life possible. By representing what others believe, want, know, and feel, people can predict and explain behavior, cooperate, communicate, teach, empathize, and also deceive, so theory of mind is foundational to social cognition and to the development of the social self. In developmental psychology, the emergence of theory of mind around age four, measured by false-belief tasks, is a landmark of cognitive development. The concept has been especially influential in autism research, where the finding by Baron-Cohen, Leslie, and Frith that many autistic children struggle with false-belief tasks gave rise to the influential idea of a theory-of-mind difficulty, sometimes called mindblindness, though this is now seen as one factor among several and is debated. Theory of mind also frames deep questions in comparative cognition about whether and to what extent other animals understand minds, and in philosophy about how we know other minds at all. As the capacity that lets us understand one another as thinking beings, theory of mind is fundamental to psychology and cognitive science.

working.text: model that another person has beliefs and desires that may differ from your own and from reality.
check whether a child can predict that someone will act on a false belief, as in the Sally-Anne task.
apply the capacity to predict, explain, and coordinate with others through what they think, want, and feel.

limits: Theory of mind is a robust and central concept, but several claims around it are debated. The age at which it emerges is not a sharp line: while children typically pass explicit false-belief tasks around four, research such as that of Onishi and Baillargeon suggests infants show implicit sensitivity to others' beliefs much earlier, and the relationship between implicit and explicit understanding is contested. The influential hypothesis that autism centrally involves a theory-of-mind deficit, or mindblindness, is now regarded as oversimplified, since not all autistic people fail such tasks and competing accounts, including executive function and social motivation, also matter, so it should be presented as one debated factor. Whether nonhuman animals such as chimpanzees truly possess theory of mind is unresolved, with evidence suggesting they understand some aspects of others' minds but not others. So theory of mind robustly names the capacity to attribute mental states, understood as emerging gradually, only partly explaining autism, and uncertain in other species.
misreadings: Theory of mind does not switch on abruptly at exactly age four; explicit false-belief understanding typically appears then, but infants show earlier implicit sensitivity, and the emergence is gradual. The idea that autism is simply a theory-of-mind deficit is oversimplified, since not all autistic people fail these tasks and other factors are involved. And it is not settled that animals like chimpanzees fully have theory of mind, with evidence mixed, so treating the capacity as appearing all at once, as the single explanation of autism, or as clearly present in animals, misreads a central but debated concept of social cognition.
origin: The capacity to attribute mental states to oneself and others, named by David Premack and Guy Woodruff in a 1978 study of chimpanzees and studied in children through false-belief tasks; central to developmental and cognitive science.
